Aysun hoca is a nice person but I don't think she is a good university instructor. She is passionate and she has knowledge but most of the time she was reading from the slides and she was inadequate in answering our questions. I also feel like the English she speaks is below the college level, it felt like she couldn't scale up her English to match the college level. She was talking and lecturing us as if we were high schoolers. However, the worst thing that happened this semester was that some students had their final on 19th december and others had their final on 2nd january, which was the official date for the final. I have never encountered such a situation before and I think this is unfair to everyone who has taken this course this semester. I don't know how this was even allowed by the archeology department as well. The reason why a change for the final date was recommended in the first place was that Aysun Hoca said that the 2nd of January was her daughter’s birthday, and also, other sections were having their final on 19th December. She said she also thought it would be nice for us as well since our final is at 6pm on 2nd January. I mean, I had finals that were at 6pm or 9am or at the last day of the final period. The fact that this course had a final date that was 4 days before the final period ended and the fact that it was determined to take place at 6pm is not an argument for the instructor to request to change the final date nor the fact that the final date coincides with a day that is important to her. And when some students objected by saying that 2nd january was better suitable than having a final on 19th december, we ended up having two options to take our final exam. Some students chose to take the exam on 19th december and some chose to take it on 2nd january. The instructor prepared two different exams as far as I know but I still cannot believe how this has happened and how this was allowed by the archeology department.
I think she did a quite good job of making the course material interesting.

The way the course is structured, both in terms of content and the teaching and evaluation method makes it no different than a high school class with the instructor lecturing and the students silently listening. With such a course it is understandable that it would be quite lecture heavy but there can still be room for participation and class discussions. But the content of the course makes this impossible as the sole goal is to transfer basic information to students without actually presenting any of the debates in the field of art history or really any academic/historical perspective on any issue under the study of the field and for this reason it doesn't much feel like an actual social science course but rather a high school class. I believe that the course would greatly benefit from at least a basic level of introduction to the philosophy of art and with weekly readings of academic articles produced by art historians which would help the student better grasp the field and the contemporary discussions rather than relying on a single introduction level book that at best presents a superficial understanding of global art history. The way art history is presented in the course is totally disconnected from the rest of history, as if it is possible to disconnect any field of history from the political, social, intellectual developments of the time. The course does make references to these every now and then but they are very few in number and do not receive the deserved attention during class. Readings that connect developments in art and architecture to the broader field of history and these other relevant developments of their time would help us better grasp how and why we observe change in the field of art and architecture. It is quite ironic that a course titled "Ways of Seeing: Approaches to Art and Architectural History" does not actually present any approaches or perspectives in the field of art and architectural history to the students.
